Least squares and basis functions

Linear systems provide a common language for solving differential equations and fitting data. In a least-squares fit, the unknowns are coefficients: first a single slope, then the weights of polynomial or sinusoidal terms. Writing these fits in terms of basis functions reveals their shared geometry and leads back to differential equations, where an unknown solution can also be represented by its coefficients.

1. Finite differences and LU

Claude exercise

The finite-difference construction in Class 6 provides a concrete starting point. Approximating a second derivative on a grid produces a tridiagonal linear system, whose structure carries through the LU factorization. Here we use ; Class 6 used the opposite sign convention, .

Finite-difference system

For a two-point boundary-value problem, the equation determines the solution between two prescribed endpoint values:

Divide the interval into equal subintervals, with and . The endpoints are known, leaving interior values to determine. At each interior point, taking the difference of two neighboring first-difference quotients gives

Substituting this approximation into the differential equation gives the coefficients at each interior point. The known boundary values move to the right-hand side, leaving the system

The grid spacing controls the accuracy of this approximation. For a sufficiently smooth solution, a Taylor expansion shows that the local second-difference error is . The tridiagonal structure, in turn, determines how efficiently the resulting system can be solved.

Bidiagonal LU factors

To exploit that structure, factor the unscaled matrix as , with a unit diagonal in . Elimination preserves the neighboring-point coupling: is lower bidiagonal and is upper bidiagonal. Writing and , matching the entries in gives

These recurrences determine every multiplier and pivot, with the closed-form solution

For four interior points, substituting these values gives the complete factors

Every pivot is at least and strictly below , so each elimination step has a nonzero divisor. With the factors available, solve and then to obtain the solution of . Each bidiagonal row requires a fixed amount of work, giving work for this structured problem.

Dense inverse

The same system also has an explicit inverse, which makes the relationship between forcing and solution values visible:

Every entry is negative and nonzero, so the inverse is dense. Although each finite-difference equation couples only neighboring grid values, the solution at any interior point depends on forcing throughout the interval. The two triangular solves capture this dependence while retaining the storage advantage of the banded factors; explicitly forming the inverse requires storing all of its entries.

Grid refinement and conditioning

The cost of the structured solve remains linear as the grid is refined, while its sensitivity changes. To see this, consider the negative eigenvalues of :

On a fixed interval, their ratio gives

A finer grid therefore reduces the finite-difference error while increasing the condition number. These two effects describe the accuracy of the discretization and the sensitivity of the resulting linear solve, respectively.

2. Slope estimation

Claude exercise

The boundary-value problem determines one unknown per grid point. In data fitting, many measurements instead constrain a few coefficients. The through-origin line from Class 6 gives the simplest case: estimating a single slope and its uncertainty.

Slope coefficient

Start with observations generated from a line through the origin, with Gaussian noise added to each response:

Fixing the intercept at zero leaves the slope as the only unknown. Each is an observed input, so stacking these inputs produces a known design matrix and the least-squares objective

Differentiating with respect to the slope and setting the derivative to zero reduces the fit to one normal equation:

For example, a realization of 100 points generated with gives

All 100 observations contribute to the two sums. The estimate is close to the generating slope; its uncertainty follows from the residuals.

Standard errors and hypothesis tests

Under the independent, equal-variance Gaussian error model, the residuals determine the estimated noise variance, slope standard error, and test statistic:

Fitting one coefficient leaves residual degrees of freedom. For the realization above, the standard error is 0.0088 and the 95% confidence interval is approximately . The same estimate can then be compared with two different hypothesized slopes:

Null hypothesisTest resultInterpretation
, Strong evidence against a zero slope.
, The data do not provide evidence against the generating slope in this test.

The estimate and standard error are the same in both tests; only the hypothesized slope changes. A p-value therefore needs to be read together with its null hypothesis.

Confidence and prediction intervals

Uncertainty in the slope carries through to the fitted mean response at any specified input . Predicting a new observation requires accounting for its noise as well. Writing , these two sources of uncertainty give the pointwise 95% intervals

At the origin, the fixed zero mean gives a zero-width confidence band, while observation noise keeps the prediction band open. These intervals provide coverage at a specified input; simultaneous coverage of the whole curve requires a different construction.

Subsampling

Another way to examine the estimate is to refit the model using fewer observations. A random 50-point subset gives with a standard error of 0.0137. When the input distribution stays comparable, grows approximately with sample size, giving the scaling

Repeated subsets reveal the slope’s sensitivity to the observations included. Overlapping subsets share data and noise, so treating them as independent replications would count shared information repeatedly. Use their spread as a stability check alongside the regression uncertainty calculation.

3. Pooling and Gaussian errors

Claude exercise

The previous model matched the data-generating relationship. Now combine two groups with different slopes into one shared fit. Its well-defined minimum lets us distinguish a successful numerical calculation from a model that describes each group well.

Pooled and separate fits

Generate 100 observations in each group, using the same Gaussian noise model as before:

Separate fits recover slopes close to the two generating values. Combining all 200 observations in a one-column design matrix instead gives a shared slope between them:

Example fits for 100 observations per group. The pooled interval is nominal: it is calculated under the one-slope model.
Data usedFitted slopeSE95% interval
Group A only1.01130.0102[0.991, 1.031]
Group B only0.49780.0083[0.481, 0.514]
Both groups, one slope0.74950.0193[0.711, 0.788]

This intermediate value follows directly from the normal equation. The pooled estimate is a weighted average of the separately fitted slopes, with each weight determined by the sum of squared inputs in that group. Writing ,

The weights are approximately 0.490 and 0.510, giving . The resulting line minimizes the combined squared error by passing between the two clouds. Its distance from each group reflects the cost of imposing one shared relationship.

Residual structure

That cost is easier to see in the residuals. For observation from group , the pooled residual combines the original noise with the difference between the group slope and the fitted slope:

The extra term grows with and has opposite signs in the two groups, producing two diverging bands in the residual plot. Giving each group its own slope removes this systematic pattern. In this example, the residual standard deviation falls from about 16.0 to 5.4, close to the generating noise level of 5.

Repeated pooled subsets return slopes near 0.75, showing a stable shared-slope estimate. The residual pattern nevertheless exposes the omitted group structure: stability and residual diagnostics assess different aspects of the fit.

Two-slope design matrix

The two group-specific fits can also be written as one linear least-squares problem. Give each group its own column, using group membership to determine which slope contributes to each observation:

The columns are nonzero on disjoint sets of rows, making their inner product zero:

The diagonal coefficient matrix separates the normal equations into the two original fits. Requiring a shared slope adds the restriction . Under the stated common-variance Gaussian model, the corresponding comparison with the two-slope alternative is

The resulting provides strong evidence against a shared slope in this example. The hypothesis concerns equality between the two group slopes; the earlier zero-slope test concerned the value of a single coefficient.

Gaussian errors

The experiment also clarifies the role of Gaussian errors. Quadratic minimization gives the coefficient estimate through algebra alone. Statistical assumptions enter when assigning it a standard error, confidence interval, or hypothesis test.

With a correctly specified linear mean, errors of conditional mean zero, and covariance , the Gauss–Markov result gives least squares minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators. Assuming Gaussian errors additionally provides a likelihood interpretation and exact finite-sample t- and F-based inference. For the through-origin model, the Gaussian log-likelihood is

For fixed , the slope enters only through the residual sum of squares. Maximizing the Gaussian likelihood therefore gives the same coefficient as minimizing squared error.

Both groups contain Gaussian noise, but pooling adds an unmodeled group effect to the residuals. Residual diagnostics therefore assess the mean structure and noise assumptions together; a non-Gaussian pattern needs to be interpreted in that context.

Errors and fitted residuals

Errors are departures from the true mean; residuals are departures from the fitted mean. Because observations share estimated coefficients, their residuals can be correlated and have different variances even when the original errors are independent and equal-variance.

4. Polynomial least squares

Giving each group its own slope enlarged the model while preserving the least-squares calculation. Additional coefficients can also describe curvature within one relationship. For observations of an object’s position over time, a polynomial provides a natural extension from fitting a line to fitting a trajectory.

Curve residuals

Write these measurements as , , and let denote a candidate trajectory. Comparing its predicted position with each observed position gives the residuals and their sum of squares:

The fit chooses coefficients that minimize this total across all observations. Because the measurement times stay fixed, each residual appears as a vertical segment between a data point and the candidate curve.

Polynomial coefficients

For a polynomial model, choosing a maximum degree of gives

This expression has coefficients, including the constant term. A quadratic trajectory, such as a starting model for a thrown ball, uses and . Evaluating its three terms at each measurement time gives the design matrix. With 100 measurements, it has 100 rows and three columns:

Each row combines known powers of with the three unknown coefficients. The predicted position is linear in those coefficients, making this a linear least-squares problem even though the curve is quadratic in time.

Notation: counts observations and counts coefficients. The multicolumn example in the Class 6 notes used these two letters in the opposite roles.

Observation count and uniqueness

The number of coefficients determines the family of candidate curves, while the observations constrain their values. In the usual fitting case, . A unique coefficient estimate requires the columns of to be linearly independent, a condition that depends on the basis values as well as the matrix dimensions.

Keeping that rank condition in view, the observation and coefficient counts distinguish three cases:

DimensionsTypical interpretation, with the relevant rank condition
An overdetermined system. Full column rank gives a unique least-squares coefficient vector; an exact fit need not exist.
A square system. If is invertible, the observations determine one exact interpolant in the chosen function space.
An underdetermined system. A nontrivial null space allows different coefficient vectors to produce the same sampled predictions.

For a quadratic, three distinct measurement times give a square, three-coefficient interpolation problem. With only two distinct times, multiple quadratics can pass through the observations.

Regularization

When the number of coefficients exceeds the number of observations, an additional preference can guide the fit. With 100 predictors and 50 observations, for example, a penalty can favor a smaller set of active predictors. The lasso expresses this preference through

The penalty favors sparse coefficient vectors, and controls its strength relative to the data-fitting term. The number of nonzero coefficients emerges from that tradeoff. Predictor scales and the relative sizes of the two objective terms therefore matter when choosing the penalty strength.

5. Basis functions and projection

The columns in the polynomial design matrix come from evaluating the functions 1, , and its higher powers. Naming those functions separately from their coefficients makes the construction reusable: a different family of functions can be evaluated and fitted in the same way.

Basis expansion

For fixed functions chosen to form a basis, write the candidate fit as

Here each is a known function, and each entry of is its unknown weight. The polynomial model is recovered by choosing

These monomials form a basis for polynomials of degree at most , giving every polynomial in that space a unique coefficient representation. Another basis for the same space would give different coordinates for the same functions. Choosing a different space, such as a finite span of sines, instead changes the family of candidate fits.

Design matrix

The design matrix connects this function representation to the observations. Evaluate each basis function at each measurement time:

Row supplies the basis values for one prediction, while column records one basis function across the entire dataset. Multiplying the matrix by the coefficient vector therefore evaluates the fitted function at every observation time:

The coefficients enter through a linear combination regardless of whether the fixed basis functions are curved, oscillatory, or localized. Their shapes determine the entries of ; their weights are determined by the fit.

Normal equations

Applying the same minimization used in Class 6 gives the normal equations for these weights:

The number of fitted coefficients sets the size of this system. A quadratic fitted to 100 measurements gives a coefficient matrix, just as the through-origin line gave a equation.

Each entry gathers information across the observations:

Thus the Gram matrix contains inner products between sampled basis functions, while contains their inner products with the data. All observations contribute to these sums. A carefully chosen basis can simplify the relationships between columns, and hence the smaller coefficient system.

Column-space projection

The equation asks whether a weighted combination of columns reproduces the observations. Least squares chooses the closest available prediction. This geometry involves two spaces: one for the coefficients and one for the observations.

Observations and coefficients

The observation vector has one coordinate per measurement, and the coefficient vector has one coordinate per basis function:

For a quadratic, contains , and contains the measured positions. The fixed times enter through the basis values in .

Columns and predictions

Each column contains one basis function’s values across the observations:

The bold denotes a whole column vector, whereas the polynomial coefficients are scalars. Matrix multiplication weights and adds these columns:

All such combinations form the column space, . Two independent columns span a plane.

Closest fitted vector

Least squares selects the prediction closest to . With minimizing coefficients , define the fitted vector and residual :

Here is the fitted function and collects its sampled values. Like , the vectors , , and belong to observation space, ; the coefficients weight the columns to determine a prediction.

Orthogonal residual

At the closest point, the residual is perpendicular to the column space. The observed vector splits into its fitted component and residual:

Orthogonality to every column gives . Substituting recovers the normal equations:

Three-observation example

With three observations, observation space is three-dimensional. Their values form the coordinates of the fixed vector . Follow how the two columns of generate predictions in a plane, then how the closest prediction is selected.

Quadratic fit in Python

Fit a quadratic to the nine synthetic polynomial observations, reproducing the degree-2 result of Find the least-squares fit. The model and its three coefficients are

The arrays t and y hold the data, and A has rows . np.linalg.lstsq finds the minimizing coefficients; the @ operator forms the predictions and inner products.

import numpy as np

# 1. The same nine observations as in the polynomial example.
t = np.linspace(-2.0, 2.0, 9)
y = np.array([5.14, 3.24, 2.30, 1.30, 1.15,
              1.10, 1.28, 2.35, 3.32])

# 2. Evaluate the basis functions 1, t, and t**2 at every time.
A = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(t), t, t**2])

# 3. Find the three coefficients that minimize the squared residuals.
coefficients, _, rank, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)
if rank != A.shape[1]:
    raise ValueError("The basis columns do not determine unique coefficients.")

# 4. Construct the fitted vector p and the residual vector r.
fitted = A @ coefficients
residual = y - fitted
rss = residual @ residual

# 5. Check that the residual is orthogonal to every column of A.
column_products = A.T @ residual
orthogonal = np.allclose(column_products, 0.0, atol=1e-11)
assert orthogonal

print("A shape:", A.shape)
print("Coefficients [a0, a1, a2]:", np.round(coefficients, 6))
print(f"Residual sum of squares: {rss:.6f}")
print("A.T @ residual is approximately zero:", orthogonal)

Output

A shape: (9, 3)
Coefficients [a0, a1, a2]: [ 1.028874 -0.406333  0.794675]
Residual sum of squares: 0.136253
A.T @ residual is approximately zero: True

The three coefficients give the fitted quadratic

The positive residual sum of squares measures the remaining discrepancy around this quadratic. The near-zero column products verify residual orthogonality, confirming the least-squares optimum for the chosen basis.

6. Orthogonality and Fourier coefficients

The polynomial fit used powers of time as basis functions. For oscillatory behavior, sines offer another choice: their coefficients describe harmonic amplitudes. They also illustrate how orthogonality can simplify the coefficient system, connecting least squares with Fourier analysis.

Sine basis

Choose the integer-frequency sine functions

Evaluating and weighting them gives the fitting function and design matrix

Each coefficient controls the amplitude of one harmonic. Adding appropriate cosine terms gives a more general finite Fourier representation, using the same construction of evaluating basis functions and fitting their weights.

Continuous orthogonality

Function inner products replace sums with integrals. For integer-frequency sines on ,

Different harmonics have zero inner products. Orthogonality separates the coefficient equations, allowing each amplitude to be computed independently.

Sampled orthogonality

For measured data, uses sums over observation times. On the uniform interior grid used below, the sine columns remain orthogonal and the Gram matrix is diagonal. Irregular times generally give nonzero off-diagonal entries, coupling the coefficients. The simplification depends on both the basis functions and where they are sampled.

Coefficient formulas

Continuous coefficients

For a target function , continuous least squares in the finite sine span gives

Each coefficient is the target’s inner product with one sine, divided by that sine’s squared norm.

Uniform sampling

At evenly spaced interior times, the discrete inner products satisfy

Fourier truncation

A numerical Fourier representation retains finitely many harmonics. Their span defines the candidate functions, and fitting their amplitudes projects the observations onto the corresponding sampled column space.

As with polynomials, choosing a finite basis converts function approximation into a coefficient problem. The same idea extends to differential equations.

7. Basis expansions for differential equations

A differential equation specifies how an unknown function and its derivatives are related. Returning to the boundary-value problem from the first section, a basis expansion represents the solution by known functions with unknown weights. Differentiating those functions gives equations for the weights, providing another route alongside finite differences.

Differentiated basis expansion

Represent the approximate solution with a finite expansion

Linearity of differentiation allows the second derivative to be taken term by term:

Each basis derivative can be evaluated directly, leaving the coefficients as the unknowns. Polynomial and special-function expansions use this construction to express a differential equation in terms of a finite collection of weights.

Coefficient equations

For example, evaluating the differential equation at selected interior points gives

Evaluating the expansion at the endpoints adds the boundary equations

Together, these rows turn the differential equation and its boundary conditions into algebraic constraints on the coefficients. The basis and the way those constraints are imposed determine whether the resulting system is square or overdetermined.

The connection with data fitting is in how the matrix is built. A fit uses values ; a differential equation can use derivatives or other operations on . In both settings, choosing a finite basis converts a problem about functions into a problem about coefficients that linear algebra can solve.

Choose a finite basis→Form equations for coefficients→Solve a linear system
